claims.text: The eutectic high-entropy alloy is multiphase and contains distinct interphase boundaries with electrochemical potential differences.
Freshly exposed interphase boundaries act as active sites for galvanic corrosion.
Continuous mechanical surface renewal and electrochemical heterogeneity synergistically accelerate both wear and corrosion at elevated temperature.
Wear-induced microcracks provide localized zones for galvanic interactions.
Mechanical wear continuously removes protective films and exposes fresh alloy surfaces.
Different phases have mismatched electrochemical potentials that establish galvanic couples at interphase boundaries.
Elevated temperature accelerates chemical kinetics and thereby increases localized corrosion.
Corrosion undermines surface integrity and consequently amplifies wear damage.
Continuous formation of fresh, more reactive surfaces accelerates corrosion.
Combined wear and corrosion will produce a higher overall degradation rate than static corrosion of the same alloy under the same temperature and environment.
The proposed mechanism applies above approximately 300°C in electrochemically active, chloride-rich media while the distinct phases remain present.
A static-corrosion sample of the same alloy at the same temperature and in the same environment serves as the no-wear baseline.
A chemically similar single-phase alloy or a modified alloy with minimized interphase boundaries can serve as a control under the same wear-corrosion protocol.
Failure of the multiphase alloy to show significantly greater degradation than the static sample would falsify the proposed primary mechanism.
Similar wear-corrosion degradation in the single-phase control and multiphase alloy would falsify interphase-boundary galvanic coupling as the primary mechanism.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis predicts and tests increases in both wear and corrosion relative to a static-corrosion baseline, but the baseline receives no mechanical wear and therefore cannot provide a matched wear response. Separate wear-only and corrosion-only controls would be needed to resolve the individual contributions and synergy.
